props.title: After Hours
props.initialSlug: A night of chaos, a life of change.

sections.content: Martin Scorsese's **After Hours** (1985) marked a radical departure from his gritty crime dramas, diving into surreal black comedy that captures Manhattan's seedy SoHo nightlife. Like a downtown twist on **Alice in Wonderland**, the film follows Paul Hackett (Griffin Dunne) through an increasingly nightmarish odyssey where every escape attempt drags him deeper into chaos. The film shares DNA with **Desperately Seeking Susan** (1985) and **Something Wild** (1986) - other 80s films exploring yuppie characters thrust into downtown subcultures, but Scorsese cranks up the paranoid tension to fever pitch.

sections.content: The film captures a specific 1980s Manhattan moment when SoHo was transitioning from artist haven to gentrified hotspot. Scorsese's camera work is relentless - prowling, swooping and diving through dark streets in ways that recall his earlier **Taxi Driver** (1976), but now with a darkly comic edge. The parade of eccentric downtown characters Paul encounters feels like a twisted tour through the era's art scene, from pretentious gallery owners to punk rockers to unstable artists.

**After Hours** spawned a mini-genre of "night gone wrong" films like **Into the Night** (1985) and **Miracle Mile** (1988), where ordinary protagonists get swept into escalating late-night misadventures. But none matched Scorsese's masterful blend of comedy and creeping dread. The film's influence can be seen in later works like **Good Time** (2017) and **Uncut Gems** (2019), which similarly follow protagonists through intense, anxiety-inducing odysseys. sections.content: The film serves as a time capsule of 1980s downtown Manhattan art culture, joining films like **Downtown 81** (1981/2000) and **Basquiat** (1996) in documenting that vibrant scene. Scorsese populates the film with actual artists and musicians of the era, lending authenticity to its portrait of SoHo's transformation. The tension between uptown money and downtown creativity that drives the plot reflects real cultural shifts happening in New York at the time.

While **After Hours** can be read as a yuppie nightmare about venturing below 14th Street, it's also a love letter to the weird magic of nighttime New York, joining films like **Night on Earth** (1991) and **200 Cigarettes** (1999) that celebrate the city's nocturnal spirit. The film's lasting influence can be seen in everything from **Fight Club** (1999) to **Collateral** (2004) - works that use nighttime urban settings as surreal playgrounds for identity crisis and transformation.
